intro.overview: Gulf Coast Healthcare Partners has a critical problem: their patient portal’s SSL certificate expired, and HIPAA auditors from the Office for Civil Rights (OCR) are arriving in six units. Protected Health Information (PHI) cannot travel over an unencrypted connection without triggering a reportable breach. Your job is to diagnose the certificate issue, remediate it properly, and document everything for the audit trail.

mentorQuote.title: Security Compliance Specialist, NEXUS Security
mentorQuote.quote: Before you touch anything, document the current state. Auditors want before-and-after evidence. Every screenshot tells a story — the story of due diligence, proper procedures, and professional remediation.

focusAreas.title: Certificate Lifecycle
focusAreas.description: X.509 certificate validity windows, expiration detection, and why expired certificates are a HIPAA compliance failure — not just a browser warning.

focusAreas.title: Certificate Signing Requests
focusAreas.description: Generating a CSR from an existing private key — the standard PKI workflow for renewal without regenerating keys or disrupting the trust chain.

focusAreas.title: CA Signing Operations
focusAreas.description: Using the Certificate Authority to sign a CSR and issue a new certificate with a 365-day validity window — the chain of trust in practice.

focusAreas.title: Before/After Evidence
focusAreas.description: Documenting the broken state before making changes — auditors require proof of the problem, not just proof of the fix.

focusAreas.title: Engagement Packet Compilation
focusAreas.description: Assembling three units of work into a single professional deliverable — the Part I (Internal Packet) and Part II (Client Deliverable) structure used by NEXUS Security for all client engagements.

content.whatYoureDoing: Downloading the Engagement Packet template, opening it in desktop Word, and setting the two document properties that identify it as yours. Five minutes, before you write a word.
content.whyItMatters: Document mechanics were the single largest avoidable point loss last term, and none of it had anything to do with security knowledge. Nearly all of it traces back to a document set up wrong on day one and never recovered. Do this first and it stays done.

steps.text: Download the template: EP_M2_GulfCoast.docx. Save it somewhere you will find it again.

Open it in desktop Microsoft Word — not Word for the web, not Google Docs, not Preview. Those cannot create the captions, cross-references and citation fields this packet is graded on. Maximize the window so the ribbon shows labels instead of bare icons.

Turn on the Navigation Pane. Windows: View > Navigation Pane. Mac: View > Sidebar > Navigation. Leave it open for the whole engagement — it is how you catch a broken heading before it reaches the Table of Contents.

Set the Author property. Windows: File > Info, the Author box on the right. Mac: File > Properties… > Summary. Word appends your abc123 to the existing author rather than replacing it. That is expected. Leave it.

Set the abc123 custom property. Windows: File > Info > Properties > Advanced Properties > Custom. Mac: File > Properties… > Custom. It has to match the kali-abc123 hostname visible in your screenshots — together they are how this packet is tied to the machine that produced its evidence.
Save the file now, and keep saving as you go.

content.title: Four Mechanics, Every Time
content.body:
Word owns your numbering, not you. Caption every figure with References > Insert Caption. Point at a figure with References > Cross-reference, set to ‘Only label and number’. Add every source with References > Insert Citation > Add New Source — tick Show All Bibliography Fields first or you cannot enter a URL. Build the reference list with References > Bibliography; the style is already set to APA. Never type a figure number or a reference by hand.

If you have forgotten how any of these work, Lab 1.3, Checkpoint 5 walks all four of them step by step.
The template open in desktop Word, the Navigation Pane visible down the left, and your abc123 in both the Author field and the abc123 custom property.

content.whatYoureDoing: Deploying the Gulf Coast patient portal container and documenting the broken state before making any changes.
content.whyItMatters: HIPAA requires documentation of security incidents and remediation. “Before” evidence proves due diligence for auditors. If you fix it first and document after, you have no proof of what the original problem was.

content.part: Part A: Deploy the Gulf Coast portal container

steps.text: Create a working directory for this engagement:
Change into your working directory:

whatThisDoes.concept: This downloads and starts a Docker container simulating Gulf Coast’s patient portal — an Apache web server with a deliberately expired SSL certificate.

Assign a friendly name for later docker commands
The Docker Hub image to pull

content.part: Part B: Document the broken state

steps.text: Open Firefox and navigate to https://localhost — you should see a certificate warning. This is your “before” evidence.

content.title: Screenshot
content.text: Capture the browser certificate error. Save as gulfcoast-01-initial-error.png

steps.text: Check the certificate dates from your Kali terminal:

whatThisDoes.concept: This connects to the HTTPS server like a browser would, grabs the certificate, and displays its validity dates. The notBefore and notAfter dates tell you when the certificate was issued and when it expired.
whatThisDoes.output: The notAfter date should be in the past, confirming the certificate has expired.

content.title: Screenshot
content.text: Capture the openssl output showing the expired certificate dates. Save as gulfcoast-02-cert-expired.png

content.title: Common Pitfalls
items: Port conflict: Stop other containers using ports 443 or 2222 before running this command
Docker not running: If you get a “permission denied” error, make sure Docker is running and try adding sudo
Take screenshots NOW: You cannot recreate “before” evidence after fixing the certificate

content.title: What You Should Have
content.text: Gulf Coast portal container running and accessible. Screenshots documenting the initial broken state: browser warning and expired certificate dates from openssl. These “before” screenshots are critical audit evidence.

content.title: Textbook Reference
content.body: Chapter 6 covers Secure Protocols and cipher suites, including how TLS certificates authenticate servers and establish encrypted connections. The expired certificate warning you’re documenting is what happens when certificate management fails — a gap between cryptographic intent and operational reality that Chapter 6’s coverage of secure protocol use cases makes concrete.

content.title: Dig Deeper
content.text: What is a self-signed certificate and when is it appropriate to use one? Research the trust implications of self-signed vs. CA-signed certificates.

content.title: That’s a Reference!
content.text: Chapter 7 discusses certificate types and PKI hierarchy. Let’s Encrypt documentation explains the value of CA-signed certificates: https://letsencrypt.org/docs/

content.whatYoureDoing: Generating a new CSR using the existing private key, signing it with the CA, and installing the new certificate.
content.whyItMatters: Certificate renewal is one of the most common PKI operations you’ll perform. Understanding the CSR workflow — using the existing private key to generate a new request, then signing with the CA — ensures continuity without regenerating keys.

content.title: Security Compliance Specialist, NEXUS Security
content.quote: The README in the PKI directory is your roadmap. Real infrastructure always has documentation — sometimes outdated, sometimes incomplete — but always your starting point. Read it before you touch anything.

content.part: Part A: SSH into the container and explore the PKI structure

steps.text: SSH into the Gulf Coast portal container (password: nexus2026):
Navigate to the PKI directory and read the documentation:
Read the README left by the previous administrator:
Explore the directory structure:

whatThisDoes.concept: You’re mapping the PKI infrastructure before making changes. The CA/ directory holds the root Certificate Authority (ca.crt and ca.key). The certs/ directory holds the server certificates including the expired portal.crt. The csr/ directory is your working space for new certificate signing requests.
whatThisDoes.output: Note the file permissions — the CA key (ca.key) is root-owned for security, while the certs/ directory is student-owned so you can write new files there.

content.part: Part B: Generate a new Certificate Signing Request (CSR)

steps.text: Generate a new CSR using the existing private key:
steps.command: openssl req -new -key certs/portal.key -out csr/portal-new.csr -subj "/C=US/ST=Texas/L=Houston/O=Gulf Coast Healthcare Partners/CN=portal.gulfcoast.local"

whatThisDoes.concept: A Certificate Signing Request (CSR) is a formal application for a new certificate. It contains your public key and identity information, signed with your private key to prove ownership. The CA uses this to issue a new certificate without ever needing your private key.

flags.description: Use the existing private key (no need to regenerate)
Provides identity fields inline (C=country, ST=state, L=locality, O=organization, CN=common name)

content.title: Screenshot
content.text: Capture the CSR generation command and output. Save as gulfcoast-03-csr-generation.png

content.part: Part C: Sign the CSR with the Certificate Authority

steps.text: Sign the CSR using the CA certificate and key (requires sudo because the CA key is root-owned):
steps.command: sudo openssl x509 -req -in csr/portal-new.csr -CA CA/ca.crt -CAkey CA/ca.key -CAcreateserial -out certs/portal-new.crt -days 365 -sha256

whatThisDoes.concept: The CA “signs” your CSR by combining your identity and public key with the CA’s digital signature. Anyone who trusts the CA can now verify your certificate is legitimate. This is the chain of trust in action.
whatThisDoes.output: You’ll see “Certificate request self-signature ok” followed by the subject line. The sudo password is nexus2026.

flags.description: Process a CSR into a signed certificate
Specify the signing Certificate Authority and its key
Generate a unique serial number for this certificate
Use modern hashing algorithm for the signature

content.title: Screenshot
content.text: Capture the CA signing command and “self-signature ok” output. Save as gulfcoast-04-cert-signing.png

content.part: Part D: Install the new certificate

steps.text: Copy the new certificate into Apache’s SSL directory:

content.title: Screenshot
content.text: Capture the certificate installation command. Save as gulfcoast-05-cert-installation.png

content.title: Common Pitfalls
items: Wrong key path: The portal key is at certs/portal.key — confirm with ls -la
Permission denied on CA key: The CA private key is root-owned. You need sudo for the signing step
Subject mismatch: The CN (Common Name) must match the server hostname in the certificate

content.title: What You Should Have
content.text: A new signed certificate installed in place of the expired one. Screenshots documenting the CSR generation, CA signing process, and certificate installation.

content.title: Textbook Reference
content.body: Chapter 6 covers applied cryptography in practice, including asymmetric key pairs and how they underpin the certificate signing workflow. The CSR you generate reuses the existing private key while the public component travels through the signing process — exactly the asymmetric key management pattern Chapter 6 describes.

content.whatYoureDoing: Restarting Apache to load the new certificate, verifying it works, and hunting for additional security findings.
content.whyItMatters: Verification proves the fix worked. Combined with your “before” screenshots, this creates a complete audit trail showing you diagnosed the problem, implemented a solution, and confirmed success.

content.part: Part A: Restart Apache and verify the fix

steps.text: Restart Apache to load the new certificate:

whatThisDoes.output: Restarting Apache inside the Docker container will close your SSH connection. You’ll see “Connection to localhost closed by remote host.” This is normal. The container may also stop.

steps.text: From your Kali terminal, restart the container if needed:

content.title: Screenshot
content.text: Capture the Apache restart and container restart. Save as gulfcoast-06-apache-restart.png

steps.text: From your Kali terminal (not inside the container), verify the new certificate dates:

whatThisDoes.output: The notAfter date should now be approximately one year in the future. Compare this with your “before” screenshot — the dates should be completely different.

content.title: Screenshot
content.text: Capture the new certificate dates showing future expiration. Save as gulfcoast-07-cert-valid.png

steps.text: Refresh https://localhost in Firefox — the expired certificate warning should be gone (you may still see a self-signed trust warning, which is a separate issue from expiration).

content.title: Screenshot
content.text: Capture the browser showing the portal without an expired certificate warning. Save as gulfcoast-08-browser-success.png

content.part: Part B: Bonus — Hunt for additional findings

steps.text: SSH back into the container and investigate the following areas. Document anything concerning in your report:
What permissions does the portal private key have? Are they appropriate?
What signature algorithm does the CA certificate use? Is it still considered secure?
When does the CA certificate itself expire?
What TLS protocol versions does the Apache configuration allow?

content.title: Bonus Discovery
content.text: SSH back in and investigate the areas listed above. Document anything concerning in your report. These bonus findings strengthen your deliverable and demonstrate thoroughness to the client.

content.title: Common Pitfalls
items: SSH session disconnects on Apache restart — this is expected behavior inside Docker. Restart the container from your Kali terminal: sudo docker start gulfcoast-portal
Certificate change not reflected — if openssl still shows the old expiration date, run docker restart gulfcoast-portal and wait 10 seconds before checking again.

Self-signed trust warning persists in browser — this is separate from expiration. Your openssl verification is the authoritative check. The browser warning about self-signed CAs is expected and does not mean your fix failed.
Missing 'before' screenshots — you cannot recreate the broken state after fixing the certificate. If you missed them, note this limitation in your report.

content.title: What You Should Have
content.text: A verified, working HTTPS connection with valid certificate dates. Screenshots showing Apache restart and successful verification via openssl. The “after” evidence combined with your “before” screenshots creates a complete remediation audit trail.

content.title: Textbook Reference
content.body: Chapter 6 covers cryptographic attacks and cipher suite weaknesses, including how obsolete algorithms remain negotiable on misconfigured servers. Beyond the expired certificate, any weak cipher findings represent the attack surface Chapter 6’s “Cryptographic Attacks” section describes — exploitable not through the algorithm itself but through how it’s deployed.

content.whatYoureDoing: Compiling all three units of Module 2 work into a professional Engagement Packet.
content.whyItMatters: This isn’t just an academic assignment — it’s a professional deliverable. In six units, Jennifer Walsh presents this documentation to OCR auditors as evidence of due diligence.

content.title: One Document, Two Parts
content.text: Your Engagement Packet is one .docx file containing both parts in this order: Part I (Internal Packet) followed by Part II (Client Deliverable). Do not submit separate files.

sections.label: Part I: Internal Packet (40% of grade)
sections.description: Timesheet (5%) — hours across all 3 units, split Internal Training vs. Client Billable. Units 1–2 (Lab 2.1 and 2.2 work) = internal training. Unit 3 (certificate remediation for Gulf Coast) = client billable. Runbook (20%) — man-page style entries for cryptographic operations (from Lab 2.1), authentication systems and SSH configuration (from Lab 2.2), and certificate remediation workflow (this unit). Commands, flags, expected outputs — enough that another analyst could reproduce your work. Analyst Reflection (15%) — honest answers to: what you took from this engagement, expectations vs. reality, how it changed your thinking, how it applies to the field. If you used AI, describe where and how you validated; if not, write N/A.

sections.label: Part II: Client Deliverable (60% of grade)
sections.description: Cover Page, Table of Contents, and Appendix are mechanical requirements (graded via deductions, not additive). Executive Summary (12%) — one page MAX but fleshed out: risk posture, findings by severity, top recommendations with business framing. Methodology (7%) — client-facing narrative of your approach. Findings (22%) — certificate issues, expired/misconfigured chain, missing controls. Numbered, severity-ordered, with evidence and impact. Risk Analysis (11%) — HIPAA implications, OCR audit exposure, patient trust impact. Recommendations (8%) — prioritized (immediate fixes vs. longer-term hardening).

content.title: Include in Part I (Internal Packet)
items:
A. Timesheet (5%)
  • Hours per unit: Lab 2.1 (internal training), Lab 2.2 (internal training), Lab 2.3 (client billable to Gulf Coast Healthcare Partners)
  • Date, specific activity name, and hours per line entry (no “did lab” entries)
  • Internal vs. client-billable split clearly indicated
  • Justification narrative for any unusual entries (very high or very low hours on a task)
  • Total hours at the bottom

B. Runbook (20%)
  • One man-page-style entry per tool used across Labs 2.1, 2.2, and 2.3 (openssl, ssh-keygen, certutil, curl, etc.)
  • For each tool: name and purpose, switches used (with one-line explanations), switches not used but worth knowing
  • How you used the tool on the Gulf Coast engagement (the actual command you ran)
  • What output came back (with screenshot reference)
  • What you did with the result (how it fed into your remediation steps or findings)
  • Bar: a colleague picking this up in 3 months should be able to reproduce your engagement

C. Analyst Reflection (15%)
  • Timesheet Self-Audit. Was there a task or section that took disproportionately long? Describe what made it slow (unfamiliar tool, certificate chain debugging, troubleshooting an error) and what you’d do differently next time. Then total your hours: if Maya Rodriguez reviewed your timesheet alongside this deliverable, what conclusion would she draw about your efficiency?
  • Professional Reflection. What worked on this engagement? What didn’t? If you ran this certificate remediation engagement for Gulf Coast again next semester with what you know now, what would you do differently? Be specific — “I’d test the chain validation earlier” is more useful than “I’d be more organized.”
  • AI Methodology Reflection. Where AI helped you on this engagement, and how you validated what it told you. Strong answers describe specific moments of help and the verification step that followed (e.g., “I asked Claude to explain an X.509 extension; I confirmed against RFC 5280 before writing my finding.”). “I didn’t use AI on this engagement (N/A)” is acceptable if true — but don’t claim N/A if your runbook is full of AI-generated explanations.
  • No word floor. No required structure. Honest reflection earns credit; filler doesn’t.

content.title: Include in Part II (Client Deliverable)
items:
Executive Summary (12%)
  • One page maximum. Hard limit — exceeding it is a Tier 2 deduction (−10%)
  • Overall risk posture in 1–2 sentences
  • Count of findings by severity (e.g., “2 Critical, 4 High, 3 Medium”)
  • Top 2–3 recommendations with business framing
  • Board-readable: no first person, no command output, no jargon unfamiliar to a non-technical executive
  • The “money page” for Jennifer Walsh — every line should tie to patient trust, HIPAA exposure, or operational continuity

Methodology (7%)
  • 3–4 paragraph narrative of your engagement approach
  • Phases of the engagement (e.g., chain inspection → root cause identification → remediation planning → certificate replacement → verification)
  • Scope and limitations: what was in scope (Gulf Coast certificate infrastructure), what was not
  • Tools used at a high level (per-flag detail belongs in your Runbook, not here)
  • Written for the client, not for security peers — this is client-facing

Findings (22%)
  • Number each finding sequentially (Finding 1, Finding 2, ...)
  • Descriptive title (e.g., “TLS Certificate Chain Contains Expired Intermediate CA”)
  • Severity rating (Critical / High / Medium / Low / Informational)
  • Affected host(s), service(s), or certificate chain segment
  • Description, including specific CVE or vulnerability identifiers where applicable
  • Evidence: reference to your screenshot(s) or openssl output (e.g., “See Figure 4 in Appendix”)
  • Impact statement in business terms (what could happen to Gulf Coast operations or HIPAA posture)
  • Per-finding recommendation summary (one line — full remediation lives in Recommendations)
  • Order findings by severity, highest first

Risk Analysis (11%)
  • Per-finding likelihood × impact analysis
  • Business context for Gulf Coast specifically: healthcare, HIPAA exposure, OCR audit risk, patient data sensitivity
  • Answer “so what?” for each finding — why does this matter to Jennifer’s organization
  • Differentiated reasoning per finding (avoid uniform “high risk” labels with no logic)
  • Reference an authoritative risk framework where helpful (NIST SP 800-30, HIPAA Security Rule risk analysis requirements)

Recommendations (8%)
  • Prioritized: Monday-morning fixes (low effort, immediate impact) vs. next-quarter budget items (higher effort, strategic)
  • Each recommendation specific: what to do, what effort required, what priority window
  • Aligned with findings (each recommendation maps to one or more findings)
  • Acknowledge client constraints — Jennifer’s team has limited capacity; recommendations should be feasible
  • Where applicable, indicate which control framework the recommendation aligns with (NIST SP 800-52 for TLS, HIPAA Security Rule, NIST CSF)

content.title: Runbook Format: Like a Man Page
content.body: Per-tool entry, structured: Name (tool and basic purpose). Description (what it does, when you’d reach for it). Switches used (each flag you used on Gulf Coast with a one-line explanation). Switches for future use (flags you didn’t use this time but should know). How you used it (your actual command). What came back (the output, with screenshot reference). What you did with it (how the result fed into your findings). Bar: a colleague picking this up in 3 months should be able to reproduce your engagement.

content.title: Analyst Reflection: Honest, Not Performative
content.body:
Real questions for real answers. Graders can tell when reflection is filler. Honest reflection earns credit — even short, honest reflection. Answer:
  • What did you take from this engagement specifically?
  • Did you have expectations going in? Verified or smashed?
  • Has this changed how you think about cryptography, authentication, or compliance work?
  • Can you see how the work applies to the field outside this course?
  • What from this engagement will serve you in the future?
  • If you used AI tools: where, how, and how did you validate? If not, write N/A.
No minimum word count. No required structure. Genuine reflection.

content.title: Executive Summary Tips
content.text: Write for Jennifer Walsh (CISO), not technical staff. Lead with finding and fix, not methodology.

content.title: Common Pitfalls
items: PDF submission: Must be .docx — PDF submissions receive automatic zero
Missing VM name: Every screenshot must show your hostname (kali-)
Fewer than 10 references: Man pages, RFCs, CVE entries, and vendor/NIST documentation all count. The textbook does NOT — see the Citations page

content.title: What You Should Have
content.text: A complete Engagement Packet in .docx format containing all 12 required sections, 25+ screenshots, and minimum 10 references.

content.title: Textbook Reference
content.text: Chapter 11 covers compliance requirements for healthcare systems. Your remediation documentation demonstrates due diligence — exactly what HIPAA auditors expect.
content.body: Chapter 11’s “Cloud vs. On-premises Requirements” section is directly relevant here: Gulf Coast’s patient portal runs in a container now, but the authentication and compliance controls you’re documenting must account for where systems will live. Chapter 11 explains how authentication requirements shift between on-premises and cloud environments — a distinction that belongs in your professional recommendations for a healthcare client with a cloud migration ahead.

content.whatYoureDoing: Walking the finished packet end to end, refreshing everything Word computes for you, and stripping out everything that was only ever scaffolding. Ten minutes.
content.whyItMatters: Every deduction in this category is avoidable and none of it is about security. A packet that goes out with placeholder text still in it, a Table of Contents that describes an earlier draft, or a figure number that points at the wrong picture tells the client nobody read the document before sending it. They will wonder what else nobody checked.

steps.text: Refresh every field. Windows: Ctrl+A then F9. Mac: ⌘A then F9. If nothing happens, your function keys are set to media controls — hold Fn as well, or use the Fn Lock key.
Rebuild the Table of Contents. Right-click it and choose Update Field > Update entire table. Not ‘page numbers only’ — that will not pick up sections you added or removed.

Read the Navigation Pane top to bottom. No blank entries. No figure captions. Only real sections. A blank entry means an empty paragraph is carrying a heading style — click in it and apply Home > Styles > Normal. A caption in the list means it was formatted by hand instead of with Insert Caption.
Compare the Table of Contents against the Navigation Pane. They read from the same source, so they should match exactly. If they disagree, you did not update the entire table.

Click every figure number and every reference to a figure. A real field shades gray when your cursor enters it; typed text does nothing. Anything that does not shade gray was typed by hand and will be wrong the moment something moves. Replace it with References > Insert Caption or References > Cross-reference.

Rebuild the reference list. Click it and press F9, or run References > Bibliography again. Count the entries: you need ten besides the textbook, and every one of them has to appear at least once in the body of the packet. A source that sits in the list and is never cited does not count.

Replace or delete EVERY item in square brackets. Not most of them — all of them. The template ships with roughly 84 bracketed slots: some are places your content goes, some are prompts telling you what belongs there, and both are scaffolding that must be gone before you submit. Search for the bracket character itself — Windows: Ctrl+F. Mac: ⌘F — type a single [ and step through every hit. Replace it with your own work, or delete the line entirely if that section does not apply. Then search again and confirm you get zero results. The runbook skeleton and the finding card are where they hide.

Check your document properties survived. Windows: File > Info. Mac: File > Properties…. Your abc123 in the Author field and in the abc123 custom property, matching the kali-abc123 hostname visible in your screenshots.
Look at every screenshot at full size. Legible, cropped to what matters, kali-abc123 visible in the prompt. A screenshot nobody can read is evidence of nothing.
Save as .docx and submit that. Word format only — not PDF, not Pages, not Google Docs. The file’s metadata is part of how submissions are verified, and exporting to another format destroys it.

content.title: Leftover Brackets Cost You 10%
content.body: −10%, flat, triggered by a single surviving bracket. Not per-item — one is the same as forty, because the failure is the same failure: nobody read the document before sending it. A packet that reaches the client still saying [what this tool/step accomplishes and why] or [Title of your highest-severity finding] is marked accordingly. It is also the most preventable deduction on the list. Search for [ and confirm zero results before you submit.
